title: Foundations: Americana Roots - The Complete Guide
summary: What Americana Roots is, where it came from, and how its songs work.
body:
Americana Roots songs: Americana roots music blends folk, country, blues, and gospel into songs about American places and working lives — front-porch harmonies, acoustic guitars, fiddles, and plainspoken storytelling.

History: The term Americana was coined for radio format use in the 1990s, but the sound goes back to the 1920s Bristol Sessions and artists like the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers. Gillian Welch, Alison Krauss, and the O Brother, Where Art Thou? soundtrack (2000) brought it to new audiences.

How the songs work: Americana Roots favors the keys of G, D, C, A, Em. Common forms include Verse-chorus with stacked sibling harmonies; Story ballad with instrumental breaks. Players should master high lonesome sibling harmony a third above the melody first, then flatpicking fiddle-tune breaks on guitar or mandolin. Capo 2–3 for bright, ringing open-string tone.

title: Scarborough Fair - Complete Public-Domain Song
summary: Full lyrics and playing guide for Scarborough Fair, a public-domain Americana Roots standard.
body:
Scarborough Fair (Traditional English ballad. Public domain.) is public domain, so this record carries the complete lyrics — sing it, teach it, record it freely.

COMPLETE LYRICS:
Are you going to Scarborough Fair?
Parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme;
Remember me to one who lives there,
She once was a true love of mine.

Tell her to make me a cambric shirt,
Parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme;
Without no seams nor needlework,
Then she'll be a true love of mine.

Tell her to find me an acre of land,
Parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme;
Between the salt water and the sea strand,
Then she'll be a true love of mine.

Tell her to reap it with a sickle of leather,
Parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme;
And gather it all in a bunch of heather,
Then she'll be a true love of mine.

HOW TO PLAY IT: a Americana Roots accompaniment in G using the 'Americana I–V–vi–IV' pattern:
G | D | Em | C

Technique: high lonesome sibling harmony a third above the melody. Capo 2–3 for bright, ringing open-string tone.
facts: Form: Verse-chorus with stacked sibling harmonies

title: In the Pines (Where Did You Sleep Last Night) - Complete Public-Domain Song

body:

Tell me where did you sleep last night?
In the pines, in the pines,
Where the sun don't ever shine,
I would shiver the whole night through.

Her husband was a hard-working man,
Just about a mile from here,
His head was found in a driving wheel,
But his body never was found.

title: House of the Rising Sun - Complete Public-Domain Song
summary: Full lyrics and playing guide for House of the Rising Sun, a public-domain Americana Roots standard.
body:
House of the Rising Sun (Traditional American folk song. Public domain.) is public domain, so this record carries the complete lyrics — sing it, teach it, record it freely.

COMPLETE LYRICS:
There is a house in New Orleans
They call the Rising Sun,
And it's been the ruin of many a poor boy,
And God, I know I'm one.

My mother was a tailor,
She sewed my new blue jeans,
My father was a gamblin' man
Down in New Orleans.

Now the only thing a gambler needs
Is a suitcase and a trunk,
And the only time he's satisfied
Is when he's on a drunk.

Oh, mother, tell your children
Not to do what I have done,
Spend your lives in sin and misery
In the House of the Rising Sun.

HOW TO PLAY IT: a Americana Roots accompaniment in C using the 'Roots lament i–VII–VI' pattern:
Cm | A# | G# | G7

Technique: brush strumming with a light palm mute for train rhythm. Capo 2–3 for bright, ringing open-string tone.

title: Orphan Girl - Americana Roots Song Study

body:
Orphan Girl — Gillian Welch, 1996. A modern old-time song that sounds a century old.
